newsitem.title: USA: Debt help must be backed by open trade-UK's Clarke.
newsitem.headline: Debt help must be backed by open trade-UK's Clarke.

text.p: The world's trade and financial system must be more open to ensure that newly agreed help for the world's poorest debtor countries will last, UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Monday.
"Liberalisation of capital flows, like liberalisation of trade, benefits both the investor and recipient," Clarke told the International Monetary Fund development committee.
This week, the major industrial countries put their weight behind a series of moves which should allow some of the world's poorest countries to shake off the manacles of debt.
"Our major task is to find ways in which we can provide support for those poorest developing countries which are making genuine efforts to reform their economies," he said.
Finance ministers expect the first countries to benefit from debt relief to be selected by the end of the year. Names discussed include Uganda, Bolivia, Ethiopia, Guyana and Mali.

"Further trade liberalisation will supplement debt releif by helping the poorest nations to earn foreign currency to meet their residual debt repayments," Clarke said. "It should complement the debt initative, in a broader sense, by helping countries which do not qualify for debt relief."
The Chancellor said there was increasing evidence that even the poorest countries could attract private investment if the fundamentals were right.
Creditors on their part must be more flexible in how they are prepared to help countries cope with their debt.
"But dealing with the legacy of debt is only the first step on the way. The next is to ensure that unsustainable debts do not recur."
He gave his backing to proposals by the head of the World Trade Organisation, Renato Ruggiero, for wealthy countries to abolish tariffs on exports of the least developed nations.

"Although the EU's preferential market access covers 97 percent of current trade, Mr Ruggiero's new proposal would encompass products in which developing countries have more of an interest, such as agricultural prodice."
Clarke said he would press other governments to support the proposal at the WTO ministerial conference later this year in Singapore.

"The benefits of open markets...provide one of the surest ways of generating the resources that help underpin political stability and promote higher standards of living, employment and environmental protection," Clarke added.
